title: Cognitive Distillation for Information Forensics: Towards Improved Hateful Meme Detection

problem.claim: Hateful meme detection is challenging because memes are multimodal, often convey viewpoints metaphorically, and may contain implicit hateful information.

gap.claim: Most existing information-forensics methods rely only on image-text semantic similarity and ignore that meme meanings are shaped by the collective cognition of diverse users.

contributions.claim: The Cognition-driven Information Forensics framework integrates the collective cognition of diverse users into information forensics and hateful-content detection.
The framework combines diverse user-comment acquisition, feature-to-cognition alignment distillation, and dual-level association learning.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the framework significantly improves detection performance on mainstream datasets.
The authors report a 4.2% higher detection performance than the current state-of-the-art model on the FHM dataset.

narrative_sequence.summary: Hateful meme detection is difficult because memes use multimodal, metaphorical, and potentially implicit hateful content.
Evidence-enhanced methods retrieve related meme examples for analogical reasoning.
Existing methods overlook collective user cognition when conducting information forensics.
The proposed framework models collective cognition through simulated comments, cognition-aligned distillation, and dual-level association learning.
The authors report improved performance across mainstream datasets and a 4.2% gain on FHM over the current state of the art.

source_observation.claim: The framework uses diverse simulated user comments to represent collective cognition in hateful meme detection.

interpretation.claim: For multimodal content whose meaning depends on social interpretation, modeling diverse audience perspectives may complement direct image-text similarity.

application.claim: Consider incorporating diverse perspective generation and explicit alignment between content features and socially shaped semantic representations in comparable information-forensics tasks.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether simulated comments faithfully represent real collective cognition or whether the approach generalizes beyond hateful meme detection.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the mainstream datasets used beyond naming FHM.
The abstract does not provide experimental settings, baselines, statistical significance, or ablation results.
The abstract does not establish independent verification or reproducibility.
